extracted.intended_audience: general readers, educators, historians, and organizers interested in the history and structure of Soviet student academic competitions
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the organizational rules, rounds, participant eligibility, scoring, timing, and awards for Soviet-era student Olympiads at school and university levels. Useful as a reference for how multi-stage national academic competitions were structured in the USSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-round competition structure
rubrics_metrics.description: There were two separate multi-round competitions every year: for higher education (universities) and general education (7th–10th/11th grade). Both competitions had several rounds, and winners from lower rounds would go to the next round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounds are hierarchical and progressive; earlier rounds can be shorter while later rounds may be longer and more complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform problem set and individual work
rubrics_metrics.description: All students were given the same set of problems to solve and they worked on solutions strictly individually — no teamwork was allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual scores were used to compute team results; strict prohibition of collaboration during problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team scoring method
rubrics_metrics.description: Team scores were simply the sum of individual member scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team performance is an aggregate of individuals rather than joint solutions or team-based problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest parts and modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each contest could have 2–3 parts (e.g., theory, lab and computer modeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later rounds could span a week and include multiple parts; organizers choose parts appropriate to subject (e.g., lab for physics, computer modeling for programming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of school olympiads
rubrics_metrics.description: School-level competitions were organized in hierarchical administrative levels: School, District (Raion), City, Regional (Oblast), Republican and All-Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions were organized separately for every school grade; the highest round reached varied by subject and region (e.g., All-Union for Math, Physics, Chemistry; Regional for some other disciplines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate grade streams in school Olympiads
rubrics_metrics.description: The school (general education) Olympiad had separate threads for every grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each grade competed within its own channel rather than mixed-age competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: School round requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every school was supposed to have a school round competition; judges were subject teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners from this round could compete in the next round representing their schools; each grade could send 3–4 students to the next round; usually conducted at the beginning of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: District (Raion) round organization and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: District rounds were for schools in an administrative district and were organized by district education departments (RaiONOs). Participants came in teams; both teams and individuals were recognized and awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners formed area teams (3–4 students from every grade). Area rounds on each subject usually took place on different days, letting students enter multiple subjects. Typically held in the first half of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: City round organization and scheduling constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: City rounds were for students of large cities and organized by city education departments (GorONO). Winners from the previous round could participate; winners formed teams to represent the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contests on different subjects were conducted on the same day at city rounds, so a student could usually compete in only one subject. In some places this round was skipped; usually held in the first half of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional (Oblast) round composition and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional rounds were for students of the whole region (oblast) and organized by regional education councils (OblONO). Winners from previous rounds could participate; winners formed teams to represent the region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional rounds included winners of the Kvant magazine competition and winners of the republican and All-Union olympiads of the previous year; usually conducted in the second half of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican round role and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republican round recognized the best students of the Soviet republics and was organized by Republican Ministries of Education. Winners formed teams and advanced to the next round representing their republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Russia the competition was conducted in four zones; some entities (Moscow, Leningrad, specialized mathematical schools, transportation ministry schools) did not compete at the republican level and sent teams directly to the All-Union round. Usually conducted in the second half of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-Union round as national final
rubrics_metrics.description: The All-Union round was the final round recognizing the best students of the Soviet Union in each subject for every grade. It was organized by the Soviet Ministry of Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This round was comparable to a national-level final and was usually conducted at the end of the school year; winners from the previous round could participate in teams and individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners were awarded diplomas; material prizes were minor and usually included scientific books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition was primarily symbolic/academic rather than material; diplomas were the main official award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence Olympiads and Kvant magazine pathway
rubrics_metrics.description: There were correspondence Olympiads organized by newspapers, journals and universities (notably Kvant magazine). Winners of Kvant competitions were admitted to the Republican round of the All-Union Physics and Mathematics Olympiads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondence competitions provided an alternative qualification pathway into higher rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: School team contests and specialized events
rubrics_metrics.description: There were team contests organized for schools to compete for District, City or Regional honors; specialized contests included the 'Physics fight' organized by Moscow State University and city-level interdisciplinary contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team contests coexisted with individual formats; cities also ran interdisciplinary events like the 'Lomonosov tour'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Contests were conducted in many subjects of the Soviet school and higher-education curriculum such as Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Programming, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some subjects (Math, Physics, Chemistry) tended to reach higher rounds (All-Union) more commonly than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: University Olympiad structure
rubrics_metrics.description: University-level Olympiads had University, Republican and All-Union rounds; there was one contest for all students regardless of year in the university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University rounds were usually organized by faculty staff (judges) and typically held at the beginning of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: University Republican round team size
rubrics_metrics.description: In the university Republican round teams had up to a dozen students each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican round was organized by Republican Ministries of Education and usually conducted in the second half of the school year.

rubrics_metrics.name: University All-Union round team composition and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The university All-Union round was the final round for university students; teams had 4–5 members and the round was usually conducted at the beginning of the next school year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners from previous rounds could participate in teams and individually; organized by the Soviet Ministry of Education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of problems and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems (and their solutions) from some Olympiads — e.g., Moscow joint Olympiads in Linguistics and Mathematics — were published in the Science and Life (Наука и Жизнь) popular science magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of problems served both dissemination and prestige; published problems could be used to admit winners from external competitions (e.g., Kvant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and timing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical timing: school round at beginning of school year; district and city rounds in the first half; regional and republican rounds in the second half; All-Union usually at the end of the school year (university All-Union sometimes at start of next school year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier rounds could take just one session, while later rounds might span a week with multiple parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary and experimental olympiad formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments such as joint 'Olympiads in Linguistics and Mathematics' challenged students in both domains on the same contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These events argued for cross-domain logical reasoning and sometimes resulted in published problem sets; they represent a flexible deviation from strict single-subject formats.
